question:
Select the most appropriate meaning of the underlined idiom.
Coming from the movie around midnight, the boys hit the sack.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. went to sleep.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Hit the sack" means to go to bed or go to sleep, especially because one is very tired. (सोने जाना)
◦ Example: After the long journey, I was exhausted and decided to hit the sack early.

• The phrase comes from the old practice of stuffing mattresses (sacks) with straw or hay — going to bed literally meant lying down on the "sack".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To jump with joy (खुशी से उछलना): To be extremely happy or excited about something.

• Option 3: To hit a wall (रुकावट का सामना करना): To suddenly be unable to make further progress; to face a difficult obstacle.

• Option 4: To shout at parents: A plain literal action with no idiomatic meaning; it is unrelated to "hit the sack".

NOTE

• Other sleep-related idioms frequently asked in SSC exams: "To sleep like a log" (to sleep very soundly), "To catch forty winks" (to take a short nap), and "To burn the midnight oil" (to work/study late into the night, i.e., NOT sleeping).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who always expects the worst possible outcome
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Pessimist.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Pessimist means one who always expects the worst possible outcome or takes a gloomy view of things. (निराशावादी)
◦ Example: Being a pessimist, he was sure the project would fail even before it began.

• The word comes from the Latin pessimus, meaning "worst".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Optimist (आशावादी): One who always expects the best possible outcome; the exact opposite of a pessimist.

• Option 3: Preacher (उपदेशक): One who delivers religious or moral sermons/lectures.

• Option 4: Serial killer: A person who murders multiple people, usually in a similar manner; unrelated to expecting outcomes.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutions often asked: Cynic (one who believes people are motivated purely by self-interest), Fatalist (one who believes events are predetermined and cannot be changed), and Altruist (one who is unselfishly concerned for others).

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One who is bad in spellings
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Cacographer.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Cacographer means one who is bad at spelling or has poor handwriting. (गलत वर्तनी लिखने वाला)
◦ Example: As a confessed cacographer, he always ran his emails through a spell-checker.

• The word is built from the Greek prefix "caco-" (bad) + "grapho" (to write) — literally "bad writing".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Cartographer (मानचित्रकार): One who draws or makes maps.

• Option 3: Chauffeur (ड्राइवर): A person employed to drive a private motor car.

• Option 4: Calligrapher (सुलेखक): One who practises the art of beautiful, decorative handwriting — the near-opposite of a cacographer.

NOTE

• Other "-grapher" one-word substitutes: Biographer (one who writes about another's life), Choreographer (one who designs dance steps), Lexicographer (one who compiles dictionaries).

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Diminutive
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. Miniature.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Diminutive means remarkably small in size; tiny. (छोटा, लघु)
◦ Example: She lived in a diminutive cottage at the edge of the village.

• Miniature carries the same core meaning of being very small in scale, making it the closest synonym among the given options.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Enormous (विशाल): Very large in size; the opposite (antonym) of diminutive.

• Option 3: Propaganda (दुष्प्रचार): Information, especially biased or misleading, used to promote a political cause or point of view.

• Option 4: Distinguish (अंतर करना): To recognise or treat as different; to tell apart.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "diminutive": petite, minute, tiny, minuscule, dinky. Its antonyms include huge, gigantic, colossal, immense.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word.
The teacher was accused of brazen favouritism in assigning the grades.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Unashamed.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Brazen means bold and shameless; unashamedly open about something considered wrong. (निर्लज्ज, ढीठ)
◦ Example: His brazen lie in front of the whole class shocked the teacher.

• Unashamed matches this sense of showing no shame or embarrassment about one's conduct, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Modest (विनम्र): Not boastful or arrogant; having a moderate estimate of one's own abilities — the opposite of brazen.

• Option 2: Shy (शर्मीला): Nervous or timid in the company of others; again the opposite of brazen.

• Option 4: Ashamed (शर्मिंदा): Feeling embarrassment or guilt — the direct antonym of "unashamed" and therefore of "brazen".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "brazen": audacious, bold, shameless, impudent, insolent. Commonly confused antonym pairs like this (brazen vs. modest/shy/ashamed) are a favourite SSC trap — read the underlined word's tone carefully before matching.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Lewis can handle many of the European languages with its dialectical varieties fluently.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. with their dialectical varieties.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The possessive pronoun "its" in the original sentence wrongly refers back to "the European languages", which is a plural noun; a plural antecedent requires the plural possessive "their", not the singular "its".

• Rule — Pronoun-Antecedent Agreement: A pronoun must agree in number with the noun it refers to. Since "languages" (plural) is what possesses the "dialectical varieties", the correct possessive pronoun is "their".

• Applying the rule: "with its dialectical varieties" is corrected to "with their dialectical varieties", correctly agreeing with the plural "languages".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "on its dialectical varieties" is incorrect because the preposition "on" does not fit the meaning (one handles a language "with", i.e. "along with", its varieties), and "its" still wrongly agrees with a singular noun.

• Option 3: "with a dialectical varieties" is incorrect because the singular article "a" cannot be used before the plural noun "varieties".

• Option 4: "with they dialectical varieties" is incorrect because "they" is a subject pronoun and cannot be used in the possessive position before a noun; the possessive form "their" is required.

NOTE

• Commonly confused pronoun sets tested by SSC: it/its/itself (singular, non-human), they/their/them (plural), and he/his/him vs she/her/herself (singular, human). Always trace the pronoun back to its antecedent noun and match number and gender.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the underlined word in the given sentence.
The ruins of this building do tell us the story of a defunct organisation.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. obsolete.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Defunct means no longer existing, functioning, or in use. (अस्तित्वहीन, बंद हो चुका)
◦ Example: The once-famous factory is now defunct and lies in ruins.

• Obsolete carries the same sense of something that has fallen out of existence or use, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: Ancient (प्राचीन): Belonging to the very distant past; something can be ancient and still exist or function today, so it is not a precise synonym of "defunct".

• Option 3: Contemporary (समकालीन): Belonging to the present time; living or occurring at the same time — nearly opposite in sense to "defunct".

• Option 4: Prominent (प्रमुख): Important, well-known, or noticeable — unrelated to the idea of ceasing to exist.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "defunct": extinct, dead, inoperative, non-existent. Do not confuse it with "ancient", which describes age, not whether something still exists or functions.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
Despite having a broken leg, Sarah managed to finish the marathon on record time.
option_1: finish the marathon in record time
option_2: finish a marathon on record time
option_3: finish the marathon to record time
option_4: finish the marathon at record time
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. finish the marathon in record time.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Preposition of Time/Duration: The fixed expression "in record time" (meaning "unusually quickly, faster than the usual time taken") always takes the preposition "in", never "on", "to", or "at".

• Applying the rule: "finish the marathon on record time" is corrected to "finish the marathon in record time".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "finish a marathon on record time" is incorrect because it changes "the marathon" (a specific marathon already referred to) to "a marathon", and it still retains the wrong preposition "on".

• Option 3: "finish the marathon to record time" is incorrect because the preposition "to" does not collocate with "record time" in this sense.

• Option 4: "finish the marathon at record time" is incorrect because the preposition "at" is used for a specific point of time (e.g., "at 5 o'clock"), not for describing the speed/duration of an action.

NOTE

• Fixed prepositional phrases frequently tested by SSC: "in time" (early enough), "on time" (punctually, at the scheduled time), "in no time" (very quickly), and "in record time" (unusually fast).

question:
Select the option that expresses the given sentence in active voice.
His wife was killed by him.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. He killed his wife.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "His wife was killed by him" is in the Passive Voice, Simple Past Tense (structure: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject).

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject
◦ Active: Subject + V2 (past form) + Object

• Applying the rule: the agent "him" becomes the subject "He"; the past participle "killed" (V3) is converted to its simple past form "killed" (V2, same form for this verb); and the subject "his wife" of the passive sentence becomes the object.
◦ Active: He killed his wife.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because "Him" is an object-case pronoun and cannot be used as the subject of a sentence; the correct subject form is "He".

• Option 2 is incorrect because "has killed" is the Present Perfect Tense, whereas the given passive sentence is in the Simple Past Tense.

• Option 4 is incorrect because "kills" is the Simple Present Tense, not matching the Simple Past Tense of the original sentence.

NOTE

• Always match the tense of the active-voice answer to the tense signalled by the passive auxiliary: "was/were + V3" → Simple Past; "is/am/are + V3" → Simple Present; "has/have been + V3" → Present Perfect.

question:
Select the option that can be used as a one-word substitute for the given group of words.
One's relatives or family, related
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Kin.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Kin means one's family or relatives; related by blood or marriage. (रिश्तेदार, कुटुंब)
◦ Example: All her kin gathered at the ancestral home for the festival.

• The word is also used as an adjective, as in "next of kin", meaning one's closest living relative.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Kilt: A knee-length pleated skirt, traditionally worn by men as part of Scottish Highland dress.

• Option 2: Kindle: To light a fire, or to arouse a feeling/interest; also the name of an e-reader device.

• Option 4: Kine: An archaic plural form of "cow", meaning cattle.

NOTE

• Related one-word substitutes: Kinship (the state of being family-related), Sibling (a brother or sister), and Progeny (one's offspring or descendants).

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined segment in the given sentence.
She is not as cleverest as John.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. as clever as.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — "as + Positive Degree + as": When two persons or things are compared and found to be equal (or unequal, in the negative), the positive degree of the adjective is used in the structure "as + adjective + as" — never the comparative or superlative degree.

• The given sentence wrongly uses the superlative form "cleverest" inside the "as...as" structure, which is grammatically incorrect.

• Applying the rule: "as cleverest as" is corrected to "as clever as", using the positive degree "clever".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "clever" is incorrect because it drops the "as...as" structure entirely, breaking the comparison.

• Option 3: "cleverest" is incorrect because it repeats the same superlative-degree error found in the original sentence.

• Option 4: "cleverer by" is incorrect because the comparative degree "cleverer" takes "than", not "by", and in any case does not fit the "as...as" equality structure implied by the sentence.

NOTE

• Degrees of comparison rules often tested by SSC: Positive (as...as), Comparative (...er...than / more...than), Superlative (the...est / the most...). Mixing degrees within one comparative structure is a very common SSC error-spotting trap.

question:
Identify the INCORRECTLY spelt word in the following sentence and select its correct spelling from the given options.
The preview version will give you a glimpse of the entaire book.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Entire.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The word "entaire" used in the given sentence is misspelt; its correct spelling is "entire", meaning whole; complete; with no part left out. (संपूर्ण)
◦ Example: She read the entire book in a single sitting.

• Spelling key: EN + TIRE. Note there is no "a" after "ent-"; the word is simply "entire", not "entaire".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "glimse" — incorrect; the correctly spelt word already appearing in the sentence is "glimpse" (with a "p"), not "glimse".

• Option 2: "preveiw" — incorrect; the correctly spelt word already appearing in the sentence is "preview" ("vi", not "vei"), not "preveiw".

• Option 3: "varsion" — incorrect; the correctly spelt word already appearing in the sentence is "version" (with an "e", not an "a"), not "varsion".

NOTE

• This question tests only the word "entaire", which is the sole misspelt word in the given sentence; "preview", "version" and "glimpse" are all already spelt correctly in the sentence itself, so their distractor forms in the options must be rejected.

• Commonly confused "-ire" endings in SSC spelling questions: entire, acquire, require, inspire, desire — always end in "-ire", not "-aire" (except genuine "-aire" words like "questionnaire" and "millionaire").

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Camouflage
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. Disguise.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Camouflage means to hide or disguise the presence of a person, animal, or object by covering it or colouring it to blend in with its surroundings. (छलावरण, भेस बदलना)
◦ Example: The chameleon can camouflage itself against almost any background.

• Disguise shares the same core meaning of concealing one's true appearance or identity, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Sabotage (तोड़फोड़): To deliberately damage, destroy, or obstruct something, especially for political or military advantage.

• Option 2: Execute (क्रियान्वित करना): To carry out or put into effect a plan, order, or course of action; also, to put a condemned person to death.

• Option 3: Gigantic (विशालकाय): Of very great size; enormous.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "camouflage": mask, conceal, cloak, screen, cover up. Its antonyms include reveal, expose, uncover, unmask.

question:
Select the most appropriate synonym of the given word.
Conspicuous
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Obvious.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Conspicuous means standing out so as to be clearly visible; easily noticed; attracting attention. (स्पष्ट, ध्यान खींचने वाला)
◦ Example: Her bright red coat made her conspicuous in the crowd.

• Obvious carries the same sense of being clearly evident or noticeable, making it the closest synonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Opaque (अपारदर्शी): Not able to be seen through; not transparent — an unrelated physical property.

• Option 2: Unnoticeable (अलक्षित): Not easily seen or noticed — the direct antonym of "conspicuous".

• Option 4: Effective (प्रभावी): Successful in producing a desired or intended result; unrelated to visibility.

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "conspicuous": noticeable, prominent, striking, salient, blatant. Its antonyms include inconspicuous, unnoticeable, hidden, obscure.

question:
Select the option that expresses the following sentence in passive voice.
The storm uprooted a large number of trees yesterday.
option_1: Large number of trees were uprooted by the storm yesterday.
option_2: A large number of trees was uprooted by the storm yesterday.
option_3: Trees was uprooted yesterday in a large number by the storm.
option_4: A large number of trees were uprooted by the storm yesterday.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 4 i.e. A large number of trees were uprooted by the storm yesterday.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence "The storm uprooted a large number of trees yesterday" is an assertive sentence in the Simple Past Tense.

• Rule — Simple Past Tense:
◦ Active: Subject + V2 + Object
◦ Passive: Object + was/were + V3 + by + Subject

• Rule — Subject-Verb Agreement with "a number of": The phrase "a number of + plural noun" always takes a plural verb, because the emphasis is on the plural noun ("trees"), not on "number". Hence the auxiliary must be "were", not "was".

• Applying the rules: the object "a large number of trees" becomes the subject, taking the plural auxiliary "were"; the verb "uprooted" (V2) becomes the past participle "uprooted" (V3, same form); and "the storm" becomes the agent with "by".
◦ Passive: A large number of trees were uprooted by the storm yesterday.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 4.

Additional Information

• Option 1 is incorrect because it drops the article "A" before "large number of trees", making the subject grammatically incomplete.

• Option 2 is incorrect because it uses the singular auxiliary "was" with the plural-sense phrase "a large number of trees", violating the "a number of + plural verb" rule.

• Option 3 is incorrect because it uses the singular auxiliary "was" with the plural subject "Trees", and it also unnaturally splits and reorders the phrase "in a large number", disturbing the correct sentence structure.

NOTE

• Distinguish "a number of" (= many; always plural verb, e.g. "A number of students were absent") from "the number of" (= the total count; always singular verb, e.g. "The number of students was fifty").

question:
Parts of a sentence are given below in jumbled order. Arrange the parts in the correct order to form a meaningful sentence.
P. provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible
Q. which can be used to satisfy our needs
R. and culturally acceptable can be termed as 'Resource'
S. everything available in our environment
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. SQPR.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Part S ("everything available in our environment") is the natural starting point, introducing the subject of the sentence.

• Part Q ("which can be used to satisfy our needs") logically follows S, adding a relative clause that describes this "everything".

• Part P ("provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible") follows next, introducing the conditions attached to the subject using "provided".

• Part R ("and culturally acceptable can be termed as 'Resource'") completes the list of conditions begun in P (joined by "and") and supplies the main verb phrase "can be termed as 'Resource'" that finishes the sentence.

• Reading the parts in this order gives a complete, meaningful sentence: "Everything available in our environment which can be used to satisfy our needs, provided it is technologically accessible, economically feasible and culturally acceptable, can be termed as 'Resource'."

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. SQPR.

Additional Information

• Option 1: SPRQ is incorrect because it places the "provided" condition (P) immediately after S, before the descriptive relative clause Q, breaking the logical flow.

• Option 3: QRSP is incorrect because it begins with Q, which contains the relative pronoun "which" and therefore cannot be the opening part of the sentence — a relative clause needs an antecedent noun to refer back to.

• Option 4: QSPR is incorrect for the same reason as Option 3 — it opens with Q, whose "which" has no preceding noun to attach to.

NOTE

• In para-jumble questions, always find the part that can grammatically stand first — it usually introduces the subject without starting with a pronoun ("which", "it", "this") or a conjunction ("and", "but") that needs something before it.

question:
Select the most appropriate ANTONYM of the given word.
Fierce
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. Gentle.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Fierce means having or displaying an intense or ferocious aggressiveness; violent, savage. (उग्र, हिंसक)
◦ Example: The fierce dog snarled at every stranger who approached the gate.

• Gentle means mild, calm, and kind in manner; not harsh or violent, which is the direct opposite of "fierce", making it the correct antonym.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: Sore (पीड़ादायक): Painful or aching, especially from injury; not an antonym of "fierce".

• Option 3: Vast (विशाल): Extremely large in area or extent; describes size, not temperament.

• Option 4: Noisy (शोरगुल वाला): Making or characterised by a lot of noise; unrelated to the meaning of "fierce".

NOTE

• Other synonyms of "fierce": ferocious, savage, violent, aggressive. Other antonyms: mild, tame, calm, meek, docile.

question:
Select the most appropriate idiom to fill in the blank.
Her son came from Europe to meet her ________ after 20 years.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. out of the blue.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The idiom "Out of the blue" means suddenly and unexpectedly, without any warning. (अचानक, बिना किसी पूर्व सूचना के)
◦ Example: After years of silence, he called me out of the blue last night.

• In the given sentence, the son's visit after a gap of 20 years fits the sense of an unexpected, unannounced arrival, making "out of the blue" the most appropriate fit.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: To blow off steam (गुस्सा निकालना): To release pent-up anger, energy, or tension; does not fit the context of meeting a family member.

• Option 2: Like a cakewalk (बहुत आसान): Describing something very easy to do; unrelated to the context of an unexpected reunion.

• Option 4: To step up one's game (अपना प्रदर्शन सुधारना): To improve one's performance or effort; unrelated to the context of the sentence.

NOTE

• Other idioms of suddenness/surprise often asked by SSC: "At the drop of a hat" (immediately, without hesitation), "All of a sudden" (unexpectedly), and "Bolt from the blue" (a sudden and unexpected event, usually unpleasant).

question: Select the INCORRECTLY spelt word.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. Jewelerry.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• "Jewelerry" is misspelt; the correct spelling is "Jewellery" (British) / "Jewelry" (American), meaning ornaments made of precious metals or stones. (आभूषण)
◦ Example: She inherited a beautiful collection of jewellery from her grandmother.

• Spelling key: British English uses JEWEL + LERY ("jewellery", with double "l"), while American English drops one "l" and the "e": JEWEL + RY ("jewelry"). "Jewelerry" incorrectly combines letters from both forms.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "Revolutionise" — correctly spelt; means to change something radically or fundamentally (British "-ise" ending).

• Option 2: "Professional" — correctly spelt; means relating to or belonging to a profession.

• Option 4: "Conscientiousness" — correctly spelt; means the quality of being careful, thorough, and diligent.

NOTE

• Commonly confused British/American spelling pairs tested by SSC: jewellery/jewelry, colour/color, organise/organize, travelled/traveled, centre/center.

question:
Select the most appropriate option that can substitute the underlined words in the given sentence.
Himanshu is braver than intelligent.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. more brave than intelligent.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• Rule — Comparing Two Different Qualities of the Same Subject: When two different qualities/adjectives of the same person or thing are compared with each other (rather than comparing the same quality across two subjects), the comparative form "more + adjective + than + adjective" must be used for BOTH adjectives — the inflected "-er" form (e.g. "braver") is not used, even for adjectives that normally take "-er" in ordinary comparisons.

• Applying the rule: since "brave" and "intelligent" are two different qualities of the same person, Himanshu, the sentence must use "more brave than intelligent", not the inflected form "braver than intelligent".

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "most brave than intelligent" is incorrect because "most" is a superlative-degree marker (used with "the" for comparing three or more things) and cannot be paired with "than", which signals a comparative-degree structure.

• Option 3: "braver than more intelligent" is incorrect because it inconsistently mixes the inflected comparative "braver" with the periphrastic comparative "more intelligent" — both qualities must use the same form.

• Option 4: "most brave than more intelligent" is incorrect for the same reason as Option 2 ("most" cannot combine with "than"), and it additionally mixes degree forms inconsistently.

NOTE

• Contrast this with an ordinary same-quality comparison across two subjects, e.g., "Himanshu is braver than Rohan", where the inflected comparative "braver" IS correct, since only one quality (bravery) is being compared between two different people.

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Indian culture treats guests as God and serves them and takes care of them as if they are a part and (1)________ of the family itself. Even though we don't have anything to eat, the guests are never left hungry and are always (2)________ after by the members of the family. Elders and respect for elders is a major component in Indian culture. Elders are the (3)________ force for any family and hence the love and respect for elders comes from (4)________and is not artificial. An individual takes blessings from his elders by touching their feet. Elders drill and (5)________the Indian culture within us as we grow.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 1.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. parcel.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank forms part of the fixed idiomatic expression "part and parcel", which means an essential or basic feature of something.

• Rule — Fixed Collocation: "Part and parcel" is a well-established idiomatic pair that always occurs together; "parcel" cannot be replaced by any of the other options without breaking this set phrase.

• Applying the rule: "a part and parcel of the family itself" correctly completes the fixed phrase, meaning the guest is treated as an inseparable member of the family.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "member" is incorrect because it does not fit the fixed collocation "part and ___"; while a member of a family makes sense on its own, it destroys the idiomatic phrase the passage is building.

• Option 3: "mate" is incorrect for the same reason — it does not complete the idiom "part and parcel" and does not fit naturally in the sentence.

• Option 4: "colleague" is incorrect because it refers to a co-worker, which is contextually and idiomatically unrelated to "part and ___ of the family".

NOTE

• Cloze passages frequently test fixed collocations/idioms like this. Other common ones: "by and large" (on the whole), "safe and sound" (unharmed), "null and void" (having no legal force).

question:
Comprehension:
In the following passage, some words have been deleted. Read the passage carefully and select the most appropriate option to fill in each blank.

Indian culture treats guests as God and serves them and takes care of them as if they are a part and (1)________ of the family itself. Even though we don't have anything to eat, the guests are never left hungry and are always (2)________ after by the members of the family. Elders and respect for elders is a major component in Indian culture. Elders are the (3)________ force for any family and hence the love and respect for elders comes from (4)________and is not artificial. An individual takes blessings from his elders by touching their feet. Elders drill and (5)________the Indian culture within us as we grow.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 2.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. looked.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank forms part of the phrasal verb "look after", which means to take care of someone.

• Rule — Phrasal Verb Collocation: The passage states the guests "are always ___ after by the members of the family" — the phrasal verb "look after" (in its passive past participle form "looked after") is the standard expression for taking care of someone.

• Applying the rule: "are always looked after by the members of the family" correctly conveys that the family takes care of the guests.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "brought" is incorrect because "brought after" is not a standard English phrasal verb/collocation.

• Option 2: "taken" is incorrect because the correct phrasal verb for care-taking is "look after", not "take after" (which actually means to resemble a relative in appearance or character).

• Option 4: "sought" is incorrect because "sought after" means "in great demand", which does not fit the context of taking care of guests.

NOTE

• Do not confuse "look after" (to take care of) with "take after" (to resemble a parent/relative) or "sought after" (much in demand) — these are commonly confused phrasal verbs in SSC cloze passages.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 3.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 3 i.e. driving.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank forms part of the fixed collocation "driving force", which means a person or thing that provides the impetus or motivation for something to happen.

• Rule — Fixed Collocation: "Driving force" is a set phrase in English used to describe the main source of energy or motivation behind an action or group; "force" is almost always preceded by "driving" in this sense.

• Applying the rule: "Elders are the driving force for any family" correctly conveys that elders provide the motivating strength that keeps a family together.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 3.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "deriving" is incorrect because "deriving force" is not a standard English collocation.

• Option 2: "caring" is incorrect because although elders do "care", "caring force" is not the idiomatic phrase used here; it does not fit the fixed collocation the sentence requires.

• Option 4: "diverting" is incorrect because "diverting force" is not a meaningful or standard collocation in this context.

NOTE

• Other common "force" collocations tested by SSC: "driving force" (main motivator), "labour force" (workforce), "task force" (a group assigned a specific task), "by force" (using physical power).

Even though we don't have anything to eat, the guests are never left hungry and are always (2)________ after by the members of the family. Elders and respect for elders is a major component in Indian culture. Elders are the (3)________ force for any family and hence the love and respect for elders comes from (4)________and is not artificial. An individual takes blessings from his elders by touching their feet. Elders drill and (5)________the Indian culture within us as we grow.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 4.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 2 i.e. within.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The sentence states that the love and respect for elders **"comes from ________ and is not artificial", meaning it comes from inside a person, genuinely and naturally**, rather than being imposed from outside.

• Rule — Contextual Meaning: "Within" means inside; from an inner source, which directly contrasts with "artificial" (something imposed or fake from outside) and correctly completes the sense of the sentence.

• Applying the rule: "comes from within and is not artificial" correctly conveys that the respect for elders arises genuinely, from inside a person's heart, and is not a put-on or forced behaviour.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 2.

Additional Information

• Option 1: "outcoming" is incorrect because it is not a standard English word used in this sense (or at all, as a noun/preposition here), and it contradicts the intended meaning of an inner, genuine source.

• Option 3: "surrounding" is incorrect because it refers to the environment or area around something, not an inner source of feeling.

• Option 4: "without" is incorrect because it means "outside" or "lacking", which is the opposite of the intended meaning — the passage emphasises that the respect is genuine and comes from an inner (not outer) source.

NOTE

• "Within" vs "without" is a classic contrast pair in English: "within" = inside/internal, "without" = outside/external or lacking (as in the archaic sense "do without"). Context clues like "not artificial" strongly point to an inner, genuine source.

Even though we don't have anything to eat, the guests are never left hungry and are always (2)________ after by the members of the family. Elders and respect for elders is a major component in Indian culture. Elders are the (3)________ force for any family and hence the love and respect for elders comes from (4)________and is not artificial. An individual takes blessings from his elders by touching their feet. Elders drill and (5)________the Indian culture within us as we grow.

Select the most appropriate option to fill in blank number 5.
solution_text:
The correct answer is: Option 1 i.e. pass on.

IMPORTANT POINTS

• The blank uses the phrasal verb "pass on", which means to transmit or hand down something (such as a tradition, value, or piece of information) to others, especially to the next generation.

• Rule — Phrasal Verb Collocation: The sentence states that elders "drill and ___ the Indian culture within us as we grow" — since culture is being transmitted from elders to younger family members, "pass on" is the correct phrasal verb.

• Applying the rule: "Elders drill and pass on the Indian culture within us as we grow" correctly conveys that elders instil and hand down cultural values to the younger generation.

Therefore, the correct answer is: Option 1.

Additional Information

• Option 2: "put on" is incorrect because it means to wear something (e.g., clothes) or to add weight; it does not fit the sense of transmitting culture.

• Option 3: "hold on" is incorrect because it means to wait or to grip something tightly; it does not convey the sense of handing something down to others.

• Option 4: "grow on" is incorrect because it means to gradually become more likeable to someone (e.g., "the song grew on me"); it does not fit the sense of transmitting culture to the next generation.

NOTE

• Other phrasal verbs with "on" frequently tested by SSC: "carry on" (to continue), "take on" (to accept a responsibility), "count on" (to rely on), "pass away" (to die, not to be confused with "pass on" in this sense of handing down).
